abstract: Plant-pollinator interactions depend on floral traits and background plant community properties, yet the role of nectar micronutrients in these interactions is poorly understood. Sodium is a micronutrient of particular interest because although plants need little to no sodium, animal pollinators require it. It is unknown whether sodium-enriched nectar increases plant fitness in animal-pollinated plants and how this may be affected by the broader plant community. To test this, we grew black-eyed Susan (Rudbeckia hirta) plants in sodium-enriched or control soil. We placed pairs of sodium-addition and control plants in prairies seeded with high or low diversity and measured seed set and germination rate. In a supplementary experiment, we explored differences in floral visitation. We found that black-eyed Susan plants grown in sodium-enriched soil had sodium-enriched nectar. Seed set increased in sodium-addition plants in prairies seeded with low diversity but not in prairies seeded with high diversity. Germination rate was not affected by sodium addition. Altogether, our study highlights the importance of considering both micronutrients and context dependency in understanding plant reproduction and complex species interactions.
